what_its_for: This antibiotic combination is used to treat or prevent certain bacterial infections. Common uses include urinary tract infections (UTIs), ear infections, bronchitis, traveler's diarrhea, and a type of pneumonia called Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). It works by stopping the growth of bacteria in your body. It will NOT work for viral infections like the cold or flu.
how_to_take: Take this medicine by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). You may take it with or without food, but taking it with food or milk can help prevent an upset stomach. Drink plenty of fluids (6 to 8 glasses of water per day) while you are taking this medicine to help prevent kidney problems. Take every dose at evenly spaced times each day to keep a steady amount of medicine in your body. Finish the entire course of treatment even if you feel better — stopping early can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
dosing: Your dose depends on your infection type, weight, and kidney function — always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's specific instructions. Common adult doses include: For most infections: 1 double-strength (DS) tablet (800 mg/160 mg) every 12 hours for 10 to 14 days. For UTIs: 1 DS tablet every 12 hours for 3 to 14 days depending on severity. For children: The dose is based on body weight and will be calculated by your doctor. Do not take more or less than prescribed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do NOT double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tablets and liquid at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep out of reach of children and pets. Do not freeze the liquid form. Dispose of any unused medication properly — ask your pharmacist about medication take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid prolonged sun exposure while taking this medicine because it can make your skin much more sensitive to sunlight and increase your risk of sunburn. Wear sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid tanning beds and sunlamps. Do not take antacids within 2 hours of your dose without asking your doctor. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol as it may increase your risk of side effects. Do not take potassium supplements unless your doctor tells you to. Avoid driving or operating machinery if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of the following: Skin rash, blistering, peeling, or sores in your mouth — this could be a serious allergic reaction. Severe skin reaction with redness and spreading — this could be a dangerous condition called Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Dark urine or pale stools. Signs of low blood sugar such as sudden sweating, shakiness, or confusion (especially if you are diabetic). Muscle weakness, numbness or tingling. Unusual bruising or bleeding. Decreased urination or blood in the urine. Severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody. Cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain. High fever, chills, or worsening of your infection. Signs of a severe allergic reaction such as swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Most people start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. However, you must continue taking the full course of antibiotics even if you feel better sooner. For UTIs, symptoms like burning and frequent urination often improve within the first 1 to 2 days. If your symptoms are not improving after 3 to 4 days, or if they get worse, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine should generally be avoided in the first trimester and near the time of delivery (last few weeks of pregnancy). Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits. Breastfeeding: This medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while taking this medication. Children: This medicine should NOT be given to babies younger than 2 months of age. Doses for children are based on body weight. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially low blood cell counts, blood potassium changes, and kidney problems. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and all medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.
